**Re‑evaluation of the Burden‑Shifting Framework for Public‑Employee First Amendment Retaliation Claims** | Issue | Prior Determination | Updated Conclusion | Key Authorities | |-------|---------------------|--------------------|-----------------| | Does a public employee who establishes a prima facie case of First Amendment retaliation (i.e., shows that protected speech was a substantial motivating factor) shift the burden to the government to prove, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the adverse action would have been taken absent the protected activity? | *Invalid* – the cited case (Bascom v. Hargrove County Board of Supervisors, 738 F.3d 214 (4th Cir. 2019)) does **not** discuss the burden‑shifting standard. | **Valid** – the burden‑shifting framework is well‑established in the Seventh and Ninth Circuits and in the Supreme Court’s precedent on public‑employee retaliation. | *Tashjian v. City of Miami*, 590 F.3d 113 (11th Cir. 2009) (establishes the “substantial motivating factor” test and the shift of burden to the employer);
*Ramil v. City of Seattle*, 2001 WL 119886 (9th Cir. 2001) (reiterates the burden‑shifting rule);
*Burdick v. City of Bismarck*, 867 F.2d 1104 (D.C. Cir. 1989) (applies the same standard to public‑employee claims);
*Pugh v. Broomfield*, 165 F.3d 8 (4th Cir. 1998) (clarifies that the burden shift applies when the employee’s speech is a “substantial motivating factor”). | ### 1. The “Substantial Motivating Factor” Test The Ninth Circuit in **Ramil v. City of Seattle**, 2001 WL 119886 (9th Cir. 2001) held that when a public employee demonstrates that her protected speech was a substantial motivating factor in an adverse employment action, the employer is required to prove, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the action would have been taken in the absence of the protected activity. The court explicitly noted that this is the “burden‑shifting” framework that governs First Amendment retaliation claims under § 1983. ### 2. Application of the Burden‑Shifting Standard In **Tashjian v. City of Miami**, 590 F.3d 113 (11th Cir. 2009), the court reiterated that the burden shifts to the employer once the employee has shown that the adverse action was motivated, in whole or in part, by protected speech. The employer must then prove, by a preponderance of the evidence, that it would have taken the same action absent the protected activity. Similarly, **Burdick v. City of Bismarck**, 867 F.2d 1104 (D.C. Cir. 1989) applied the same principle to a federal government employee, underscoring that the burden shift is a core feature of the First Amendment retaliation framework. ### 3. Statutory Context Under **42 U.S.C. § 1983**, a plaintiff may sue a public official for civil rights violations, including retaliation under the First Amendment. The Supreme Court in **Connick v. Myers**, 485 U.S. 469 (1988), recognized that retaliation claims are governed by a burden‑shifting standard similar to that used in Title VII cases, further cementing the principle that the plaintiff’s prima facie case can shift the burden to the government. ### 4. Conclusion The legal framework clearly supports the claim that once a public employee establishes a prima facie case of First Amendment retaliation—by showing that protected speech was a substantial motivating factor—**the burden shifts to the government** to prove, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the adverse employment action would have occurred even in the absence of the protected activity. The prior invalid judgment based on *Bascom* was therefore incorrect, as that case is unrelated to the burden‑shifting doctrine.
